stem: On the start-of-year page, a picture map has a dotted path and a square. Its key says the square means a gate. Ask: What does the square stand for on this map?
answer: A gate. The square is a picture on the map; it is not the gate itself. Access look, no score.
steps: says or points to the gate | treats the square as a mark that stands for something | the support the child used is recorded as information
samples: It stands for a gate. | It is a square.

stem: On the page, a map has an arrow that points up and the word north beside it. The pond is above the tent. Ask: Which direction is the pond from the tent?
answer: North. Access look, no score; no capital-city recall is needed.
steps: names north or points along the arrow | the support the child used is recorded as information
samples: North. | Over there.

stem: On the page, show two pictures: the old map of Boulder, and a drawing of an imagined town that the teacher says someone made up. Ask: Which one could help us find out what Boulder looked like then?
answer: The old map of Boulder. It was made to record that place; the imagined drawing was not. Access look, no score.
steps: points to the old map | the support the child used is recorded as information
samples: The old map of Boulder. | The drawing, because it has a castle and a rainbow.

stem: On the page, a picture map shows a river running past a hill. Ask: Circle the land.
answer: The hill is circled. Access look, no score.
steps: circles the hill and not the river | the support the child used is recorded as information
samples: The hill is circled. | The river is circled.

stem: On the same page, the same river and hill. Ask: Draw a box round the water.
answer: The river is boxed. Access look, no score.
steps: boxes the river and not the hill | the support the child used is recorded as information
samples: The river is boxed. | The hill is boxed.

stem: Heard from pairs on days 2 and 3 (eight pairs on day 2, seven on day 3), after page item 3: the old map of Boulder is beside the imagined drawing. Ask: Why could the old map show what Boulder looked like then?
answer: Someone made it to show that place at the time, so it records what was there; the imagined drawing was made up. Access look, no score; item 3 of the page is repaired on day 6.
steps: gives a reason tied to the map being a record of its own place | says it, points to it or draws it
samples: It was made to show Boulder then. | It is old.

stem: Invented for practice. A new card shows a trail map of a nature preserve and a world map. Mark: Circle the map that helps you find the path to the lookout tower.
answer: The trail map.
steps: circles the trail map | chooses it for the job of finding the path
samples: The trail map is circled. | The world map is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 1 group, one at a time: Why does that map help?
answer: It shows the paths. It has what the job needs.
steps: a reason tied to the job (the paths), not to size or color | says it, points or draws
samples: It shows the paths to the tower. | Because it is bigger and prettier.

stem: Heard from the day 1 group, one at a time: A new class wants to know which map is best for a picnic. Say one smaller question that could help them.
answer: A smaller question tied to what the picnic needs or what a map shows, such as: Does the map show where the tables are? Where is the shade? A question about how pretty a map is does not meet.
steps: asks a smaller question, not a statement | ties it to what the job needs or what the map shows | not about how pretty it is
samples: Does the map show where the tables are? | Which map is the prettiest?

stem: Invented for practice. A new card called Orchard Paths has four boxes: a title, a key, a compass rose and a scale bar. The key says a diamond means a well. Mark: Circle the part that tells what the diamond means.
answer: The key.
steps: circles the key box | not the title, the rose or the scale bar
samples: The key is circled. | The title is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 2 group: What does the title tell us?
answer: The place and what the map shows (paths in an orchard).
steps: says what the map shows or where | does not give the title the key's job
samples: It tells us the map shows paths in an orchard. | It tells us what the diamond means.

stem: Invented for practice. A new fairground card has a compass rose whose arrow marked N points to the right. The stage is to the left of the snack stand. Mark: Circle the direction word from the snack stand to the stage: north, south, east or west.
answer: South. North points right, so left is south.
steps: circles south | reads the rose, not the sides of the page
samples: South is circled. | West is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 3 group: How do you know?
answer: The rose: north points right, so the other way, left, is south.
steps: points to the rose | uses where north points to say the direction
samples: The rose says north is that way, so left is south. | Left on the page is west.

stem: Invented for practice. A new card shows a path that is six equal scale lengths. Each scale length stands for three blocks. Mark: Circle how far the path is: 6, 9 or 18 blocks.
answer: 18 blocks. Each of the six lengths stands for three blocks.
steps: circles 18 | repeats the labelled ground unit for each length
samples: 18 is circled. | 6 is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 4 group: What does the scale tell us?
answer: How far each length on the map stands for on the ground. Map length stands for ground distance.
steps: says the scale ties a length on the map to a distance on the ground | not only that it has marks
samples: Each length on the map stands for some blocks on the ground. | It tells how many marks there are.

stem: Invented for practice. A new card called Lake Edge has five numbered places: a boat ramp with a fish stall beside it, garden steps cut into a hillside, a bare hill, open water and a rock. Mark: Circle two places where people use or change the land or water.
answer: The boat ramp and the garden steps.
steps: circles the boat ramp and the garden steps | no circle on the bare hill, the water or the rock
samples: The boat ramp and the garden steps are circled. | The water and the rock are circled.

stem: Heard from the day 5 group: How do people use it?
answer: Boats are put into the water at the ramp; food grows on the cut slope.
steps: names what people do at a mapped place, not only what is there | says it, points or draws
samples: People put boats in at the ramp and grow food on the steps. | There is water.

stem: Heard from the day 5 group, one at a time: Point to the part of the Lake Edge card that tells you what the garden steps symbol stands for.
answer: The key. It says what each symbol on this card stands for.
steps: points to the key box | not the title, the rose or the scale bar
samples: The key box is pointed to. | The title is pointed to.

stem: Invented for practice. On the Riverbend Park card, write one word beside one place that people made or changed (such as path or pond), or draw what they did there.
answer: A label such as path, pond or field beside that feature, or a drawing of the action. A word that names only a natural feature, such as river, is not yet seen.
steps: writes or draws beside a mapped feature, not blank paper | the word or drawing names what people made or did there, not only what is there
samples: path, written beside the dotted line | river, written beside the river

stem: Room Photograph A, an empty classroom with its credit printed under it. Mark: Circle the date.
answer: The date printed in the credit line, 2026.
steps: circles the printed date | does not guess a date from the picture
samples: The date in the credit is circled. | A date that is not printed is written.

stem: Heard from the day 6 group, one at a time, on Room Photograph A: Point to who made it.
answer: The maker named in the credit line, Curio Class (the credit, not the label that says where it is kept).
steps: points to the maker in the credit line | not the keeper's label, and not a guessed name
samples: Points to Curio Class in the credit. | Points to the label on the box it is kept in.

stem: Heard from the day 6 group, one at a time, on Room Photograph A: Point to where it was made.
answer: The making place in the credit line, a school doorway (not the classroom the picture shows).
steps: points to the printed making place | keeps it apart from the room the picture shows
samples: Points to a school doorway in the credit. | Points to the classroom in the picture.

stem: Invented for practice. A new photograph card shows a boot tray with four boots. Two statements are printed under it: Four boots sit on the mat. These boots are the coolest. Mark: Put the check token on the sentence you can check.
answer: The check token on Four boots sit on the mat.
steps: check token on the countable statement | not on These boots are the coolest
samples: The check token is on the four boots statement. | The check token is on both statements.

stem: Heard from the day 7 group: What can this source help us find?
answer: Anything the picture shows that can be counted or seen, such as how many boots are on the mat. It cannot show what everyone thinks is coolest.
steps: names the checkable detail it can help with | does not throw the whole card out because of the opinion
samples: It can help us find how many boots there are. | It can show where the boots sit. | It cannot help because it has an opinion on it.

stem: Invented for practice. A new photograph card has a credit line printed under it: Photograph by Dana Whitfield, 2026, made in a school lobby. Two statements are printed under it: A window sits beside a door. This is our best room. Mark: Circle who made it.
answer: The maker named in the credit line, Dana Whitfield.
steps: circles the maker in the credit | not the keeper's label and not a guessed name
samples: The maker in the credit is circled. | The label that says where it is kept is circled.

stem: On the same card, mark: Put the token I can check this on the picture on the statement that can be checked.
answer: A window sits beside a door.
steps: check token on the window statement | not on This is our best room
samples: The check token is on the window statement. | The check token is on both statements.

stem: Heard from the day 8 group, one at a time, on the same card: Point to where it was made.
answer: The making place in the credit line, a school lobby (not the room the picture shows).
steps: points to the printed making place | keeps it apart from the room shown
samples: Points to a school lobby in the credit. | Points to the room in the picture.

stem: Invented for practice. A new Pictures Card shows a flat paper star, a balloon and a salad bowl. Mark: Circle the one that can lie flat with no gap and no stretch.
answer: The flat paper star.
steps: circles the paper star | not the balloon or the bowl
samples: The paper star is circled. | The balloon is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 9 group: Why can a balloon's skin not lie flat as it is?
answer: To lie flat, a round skin has to be stretched, folded or opened. Earth itself is not opened; only the model is.
steps: says stretch, fold or open | does not say that Earth gets gaps or holes
samples: It would have to stretch or fold or be opened. | Earth would get holes.

stem: Invented for practice. A new Mercator card shows two made-up lakes. The lake near the top edge is drawn wider than the lake near the middle. Mark: Does the drawing prove the top lake is bigger? Circle yes or no.
answer: No.
steps: circles no | does not take drawn size as proof
samples: No is circled. | Yes is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 10 group: Why not?
answer: This kind of map stretches lands that are far from the middle, so the top lake is drawn too big.
steps: says the map stretches lands far from the middle | not that the island really is bigger
samples: The map stretches lands far from the middle. | It looks bigger so it is bigger.

stem: Invented for practice. A fresh pair of world cards, one centered on a different ocean, with their credit lines. Mark: Circle the map that keeps the shapes of small places near us right.
answer: The Mercator card.
steps: circles the Mercator card | does not drop it because it bends sizes
samples: The Mercator card is circled. | The other card is circled because the first map is useless.

stem: Heard from the day 11 group, one at a time, on the fresh world cards: Read me the credit line on one card.
answer: The credit line as printed: who drew it, the year, and where it was made. It names the coastline data as its data, not as the maker.
steps: reads or points to the maker, the date and the making place | keeps the data's name apart from the maker
samples: Drawn by Lena Hart, 2026, made in a school gym. | The coastline data made it.

stem: Invented for practice. A fresh blank outline of North America has five arrows and a printed word bank of fourteen words. Mark: Write a label from the word bank at each arrow: a country, an ocean, the Great Lakes, a river and a mountain range.
answer: Five labels, one for each arrow, each the right kind: a country (Canada, United States or Mexico), an ocean, the Great Lakes, a river of North America (Mississippi or St. Lawrence) and a range (Rocky or Appalachian). Which ocean, river or range is not scored: location is not taught. Practice only.
steps: each label sits at the arrow it fits by kind | the country, ocean, lakes, river and range are each the right kind | no continent and nothing from another continent is used
samples: Canada, Pacific Ocean, Great Lakes, St. Lawrence River, Rocky Mountains. | North America at the country arrow.

stem: Heard from the day 12 group while the others write: How did the key help you find the river?
answer: The key says a wavy line stands for a river, so the label goes on the wavy line.
steps: ties the wavy line to the key | does not read a symbol as another feature
samples: The key says the wavy line is a river. | The triangles are the river.

stem: Invented for practice. A new courtyard diagram shows two benches and five trees. A picture graph beside it has five tree marks and one bench mark. Mark: Draw one more mark so the bench row matches the courtyard.
answer: One bench mark is added, so the bench row has two marks.
steps: draws exactly one more bench mark | one mark for each counted feature
samples: One more bench mark. | No mark added.

stem: Heard from the day 13 group: Which positions should a map of this courtyard keep?
answer: The positions that were seen, where the benches and trees really are.
steps: says the observed places stay as they are | not any order that looks nice
samples: Where the benches and trees really are. | Any order is fine.

stem: Invented for practice. A new zoo map has little pictures of an elephant, a tent and a cafe. A visitor cannot tell what the little pictures mean. Mark: Circle the part to add: title, key, compass rose or scale bar.
answer: The key.
steps: circles the key | not the title, rose or scale bar
samples: The key is circled. | The compass rose is circled.

stem: Heard from a second group of six on day 14: What could this map help a visitor find?
answer: The places the little pictures stand for, once the key says what they are.
steps: names what the map could help find | may add one thing it leaves out
samples: It could help find the places the pictures stand for. | The prettiest map helps with every job.

stem: Invented for practice. A fresh response card shows a path of two equal scale lengths, and each length stands for seven paces. Mark: Circle how far: 7, 9 or 14 paces.
answer: 14 paces.
steps: circles 6 | repeats the labelled ground unit for each length
samples: 14 is circled. | 7 is circled.

stem: Heard from the day 16 group on the same card, one at a time: Point to who made it.
answer: The maker named in the signed margin, apart from the park the map shows.
steps: points to the maker in the margin | not the keeper and not the park's name
samples: Points to the signed maker. | Points to the park's name.

stem: Heard from the day 16 group on the same card, one at a time: Point to where it was made.
answer: The making place in the signed margin, apart from the park the map shows.
steps: points to the making place in the margin | not the place the map shows
samples: Points to the making place in the margin. | Points to the park.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: What does the title tell you?
answer: What the map shows: a garden called Willow Garden.
steps: says what the map shows | does not give the title another part's job
samples: It tells me this is a map of Willow Garden. | It tells me what the circle means.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: What does the key tell you?
answer: What each symbol stands for: a rectangle is a planting bed and a circle is a water barrel.
steps: names what a symbol stands for from the key | does not say the key gives direction
samples: A rectangle is a planting bed and a circle is a water barrel. | The key tells me which way is north.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: What does the compass rose tell you?
answer: Which way north, south, east and west lie on the map. North is where the rose points.
steps: says it shows directions | ties north to where the rose points, not to the top of the page
samples: It shows which way north, south, east and west are. | North is always the top of the page.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: What does the scale tell you?
answer: How far one length on the map stands for on the ground: here each length is four paces.
steps: says map length stands for ground distance | gives the labelled unit, four paces
samples: Each length stands for four paces on the ground. | It tells how many bars there are.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: How far is it from the gate to the shed?
answer: Twelve paces: three equal lengths of four paces.
steps: says twelve paces | uses the labelled ground unit for each length
samples: Twelve paces. | Three paces.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, ask: Show two ways people use or change the land or water on this map.
answer: Two actions, such as growing beds beside the water barrels and putting a bridge over the stream.
steps: names what people do at mapped places | two different examples | points to the mapped feature
samples: People grow plants beside the water barrels, and they built a bridge over the stream. | There is a stream.

stem: On Map X and Map Y, two world cards, ask: Point to one thing that shows which map is the Mercator map.
answer: Map X is the Mercator map: the child points to lands near the top or bottom drawn too big (the clue the unit taught); the other is the Peters map.
steps: points to a clue the unit taught, lands near the poles drawn too big | names or points to the map that has it
samples: Map X, because the lands near the top are drawn too big. | They are the same map.

stem: On the same cards, ask: What does the Mercator map change about the world?
answer: Lands far from the equator are drawn too big; it keeps the shapes of small places.
steps: says sizes far from the middle are stretched | may add that small shapes are kept
samples: It draws lands near the top and bottom too big. | Nothing; it is useless.

stem: On the same cards, ask: What does the Peters map change about the world?
answer: It keeps sizes the same as on the globe and stretches shapes.
steps: says sizes are kept | says shapes are stretched
samples: It keeps the sizes but stretches the shapes. | It keeps everything the globe does.

stem: On the same cards, ask: Which map helps you compare how big South America and Europe are?
answer: The Peters map, because it keeps sizes.
steps: chooses the map that keeps sizes
samples: The Peters map. | The Mercator map, because it looks bigger.

stem: On the same cards, ask: Why is that map the one to use for comparing sizes?
answer: It keeps sizes the same as on the globe, so the two lands can be compared fairly.
steps: a reason tied to sizes being kept | not looks
samples: Because it keeps the sizes, so we can compare them. | Because it is the prettier map.

stem: On the same cards, ask: What is one thing the map you chose gets wrong?
answer: What the chosen map gets wrong: the Peters map stretches shapes. If the child chose the Mercator map on item 10, the Mercator answer (lands far from the middle drawn too big) is right here; item 10 carries that error.
steps: names a change the chosen map makes | does not say the map keeps everything the globe does
samples: It stretches the shapes of lands. | Nothing; it is just right.

stem: Scored on day 15 from the revised Familiar Place Map made on day 14, not asked again: look for a title, a usable key, a compass rose set by the wall north, a scale counted in whole paces, and features in their observed places.
answer: A recognizable map of the room or school part with all four working parts and features where they were seen. Accessible participation counts equally.
steps: title, key and rose that work | scale counted in whole units | features in observed places, not decoration
samples: A map of our room with a title, a key that matches its pictures, a rose and a scale of two paces a bar. | A picture of a room with no key or rose.

stem: Scored on day 15 from the picture graph made on day 14 from fresh counts, not asked again: look for one mark for each counted feature in the place the map shows.
answer: One mark for each feature the child counted, matching the child's own fresh counts.
steps: one mark for each counted feature | marks match the counts the child made on day 14 | the graph is about the place on the revised map
samples: Counted four chairs and two plants and drew four chair marks and two plant marks. | Equal rows of marks for unequal counts.

stem: On the Vermont map of 1855, enlarged, with its imprint read aloud from a transcript, ask: Point to the words that tell who made it.
answer: The imprint names J. H. Colton as the maker (accept J. H. Colton and Company). Provisional until a person reads the imprint off the full image.
steps: points to the maker in the printed imprint | not the archive that keeps the file
samples: Points to J. H. Colton in the imprint. | Points to the archive that holds it.

stem: On the Vermont map of 1855, enlarged, with its imprint read aloud from a transcript, ask: Point to the date.
answer: 1855, as the imprint prints it. Provisional until a person reads the imprint off the full image.
steps: points to the printed year
samples: Points to 1855. | Says a year that is not printed.

stem: On the Vermont map of 1855, enlarged, with its imprint read aloud from a transcript, ask: Point to where it was made.
answer: New York, from the imprint (not Vermont, which is the place the map shows). Provisional until a person reads the imprint off the full image.
steps: points to the printed making place | keeps it apart from the place shown
samples: Points to New York in the imprint. | Says Vermont, because the map shows Vermont.

stem: On the Willow Garden caption, which reads The path runs from the gate to the shed. This is the nicest garden anywhere., ask: Which statement can be checked on the map?
answer: The path runs from the gate to the shed. The other statement, nicest, is what someone thinks.
steps: picks the path statement | names the other as what someone thinks
samples: The path runs from the gate to the shed; nicest is an opinion. | Both, because they are printed.

stem: On the Willow Garden caption, which reads The path runs from the gate to the shed. This is the nicest garden anywhere., ask: What can this map help us find out?
answer: Anything checkable that the map shows, such as where the path runs from the gate to the shed, where the beds and barrels are, or how far it is.
steps: names a checkable use | does not throw the whole map out because of the opinion
samples: It can show where the path goes. | None of it is usable.

stem: On the Willow Garden caption, which reads The path runs from the gate to the shed. This is the nicest garden anywhere., ask: What can this map not show us?
answer: What someone thinks, such as that the garden is the nicest; a map cannot show that, or anything not drawn on it.
steps: names that an opinion or a feeling cannot be shown by the map
samples: It cannot show that everyone likes this garden best. | It shows everyone likes it.

stem: Invented for practice. Each pair has six credit slips: Made by Ana Brook, 1931. Drawn by Ng and Sons, mapmakers. Kept in the Maple Street Library. Held by the County Archive. Shows Pine Lake Campground. Shows Bell Cove Beach. Lay each slip under who made it, who keeps it or what place it shows.
answer: Made by Ana Brook and Drawn by Ng and Sons go under who made it; Kept in the Maple Street Library and Held by the County Archive go under who keeps it; Shows Pine Lake Campground and Shows Bell Cove Beach go under what place it shows.
steps: lays each slip under the question its words answer | a library or archive slip is never under who made it
samples: Made by Ana Brook is under who made it. | Held by the County Archive is under who made it.

stem: Invented for practice. On the hallway card, one statement is Reading here is the best. Say a new statement about the shelf, the bench or the door that can be checked on the picture.
answer: A statement a person can check by pointing at the picture, such as Three boxes sit on the shelf.
steps: says something that can be found on the picture | does not say what someone thinks
samples: Three boxes sit on the shelf. | The shelf is the nicest.

stem: On the Pickaway County map card, write the maker as the map prints it, or write not printed if the map does not print one.
answer: Kellogg and Randall, copied as printed.
steps: the words come from the printed title block, not the picture | not printed is written only where nothing is printed
samples: Kellogg and Randall | Ohio

stem: Invented for practice. On the clock photograph card, write where it was made as the card prints it, or write not printed if the card does not print a place.
answer: not printed (the card prints a maker and a year but no place of making).
steps: writes not printed | does not write the art room or the classroom the picture shows
samples: not printed | art room

stem: Press a paper cup flat. Finish the sentence: To lie flat, the skin must ___.
answer: stretch, fold, wrinkle or tear (open), said or written, or the cup shown pressed with its folds.
steps: names what the cup had to do to lie flat | does not say the cup lay flat as it was
samples: stretch | stay the same

stem: Invented for practice. On a Mercator card, Moss Island sits near the bottom edge and looks as wide as Tern Island, which sits near the middle. Say where you could look to find out which island is really bigger.
answer: The globe, which keeps the true sizes (or the true-size cut-outs laid beside it).
steps: points to the globe or to true-size cut-outs, not to the drawn card | says the card alone cannot settle it
samples: The globe. | Look at the card again.

stem: Invented for practice. A ship's crew wants to hold one compass direction all the way. Say: I think the ___ map is best for ___ because ___.
answer: The Mercator map, for holding one compass direction, because on it a course of one direction is a straight line.
steps: names the map that keeps small shapes and straight courses | a reason about the job, not the looks
samples: I think the Mercator map is best for a ship holding one direction because the course is a straight line. | I think the Peters map is best because it is prettier.

stem: Invented for practice. On Pip's labelled outline of North America, one label sits on the whole continent where a country arrow points, and one river label sits on the triangles. Write the right word from the bank for one of them.
answer: A country (Canada, United States or Mexico) at the country arrow, or a mountain range (Rocky or Appalachian) beside the triangles.
steps: the new label fits the kind of thing the arrow or symbol points to | does not use a continent or a place from another continent
samples: Canada | North America

stem: On the Pickaway County map card, write the date as the map prints it, or write not printed if the map prints none.
answer: 1858, copied from the title block.
steps: the year comes from the printed title block | not a year guessed from how the map looks
samples: 1858 | a long time ago

stem: Heard from the day 10 group, one at a time, on the new Mercator card: What does this kind of map keep right?
answer: The shapes of very small places, such as the places near us. It does not keep the sizes of lands far from the middle.
steps: says small shapes are kept | does not say it keeps everything the globe does
samples: It keeps the shapes of small places right. | It keeps everything the globe does.

stem: Heard from the day 8 group, one at a time, on the same card: Point to the date.
answer: The year in the credit line, 2026.
steps: points to the printed year | does not guess a date from the picture
samples: Points to 2026 in the credit. | Says it was made a long time ago.

stem: Invented for practice. Pip counted 4 lamps in a made-up room and drew 6 lamp marks. Say whether the marks match the count.
answer: They do not match: 4 lamps are 4 marks, one mark for each.
steps: says six marks is too many for four lamps | one mark for each counted feature
samples: No: four lamps need four marks. | Yes, more marks look better.

stem: Point to one thing in our room that our map leaves out.
answer: A real thing in the room that is not drawn, such as something small or something that moves.
steps: points to something real that is not on the map | does not point to something the map shows
samples: The pencil cup is not on our map. | The door, which is on our map.

stem: Heard on day 15 from the six not yet heard, and read from every child's day 14 claim sheet, not asked again: look for a map and a purpose that match, a because that points to something the map shows, and what the map leaves out or bends.
answer: A claim whose map fits its purpose, whose because points to a feature of that map, and that says what the map leaves out or bends.
steps: the map and the purpose match | the because points to a feature we can show | says what the map leaves out or bends
samples: I think the Peters map is best for comparing sizes because it keeps sizes, but it stretches shapes. | I think the prettiest map is best for every job.

stem: On the Willow Garden Map, an invented teaching map, turned so the rose points to the left of the card, ask: Which way is north now?
answer: Toward where the rose points, to the left of the card.
steps: ties north to where the rose points | not to the top of the card
samples: North is where the rose points, to the left. | North is the top of the card.

stem: Invented for practice. Pip says a path of four lengths, each length ten paces, is four paces long. Say whether Pip is right.
answer: Pip is not right: four lengths of ten paces is forty paces.
steps: says each length stands for ten paces | counts the lengths by tens
samples: No: four tens are forty paces. | Yes, four lengths is four paces.

stem: Invented for practice. Four slips say: North is where the rose points. North is the top of the page. The rose turns when the page turns. A rose pointing down means north is down the page. Sort each slip: true or not true.
answer: True: north is where the rose points; the rose turns when the page turns; a rose pointing down means north is down the page. Not true: north is the top of the page.
steps: sorts the top-of-the-page slip as not true | sorts the other three as true
